v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e03, writer brief a10e03-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.75 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e02's next field was honoured: an oil refinery's maintenance shutdown, and the model's working memory in plain words (what it keeps for each conversation), how much room that takes on the card, and handing that room out a page at a time. Keeps apart from a1e09 (what the model can see; here where the card keeps it and how much room each chat takes), from s6e13 (a process plant in shutdown: no grid, no control room) and from a10e01's furnace (no fired heater, furnace or oven anywhere). Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 32 layers, 8 key/value lists of 128 numbers (4,096 / 32), 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter; working memory per token 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KB; one A100 80GB shared with the document-search model (24 GB), so the program may use 56 GB: 15 for weights, 1 for working space, 40 for chats; sizes in the meter's units (1 GB = 1,024 MB). The refinery's own figures, never a source's: the program's count of 1,600 tokens for the average open chat (24 to 26 August, unchanged by the raise); the sizing sheet's 4 chats a minute from 22:00, each open about 30 minutes, so 120 at the peak and 240 of the 400 night contractors in the first hour; a question about every 10 minutes. Arithmetic (all in sims/a10e03-v1.0.0.js): sheet 1,600 x 128 KB = 200 MB, 40,960 / 200 = 204; old program 8,192 x 128 KB = 1 GB, 40 fit; 22:09:45 40 chats, 64,000 tokens, 7.8 GB (7.8125), 19.5% (19.53); 22:10:00 the 41st refused; 22:15:00 21 refused; 23:00 160 of 240 refused; 2,048 tokens 256 MB, 160 fit, peak 120 held, 30 GB reserved, 23.4 GB used, 78.1%; pages 16 x 128 KB = 2 MB, 327,680 tokens, 20,480 pages, 204 average chats, peak 120 held, 23.4 GB; two cards 80 chats, $5.58 an hour, 40 refused by 22:45 and 80 by 23:00, 19.5%; idle close 60 wanted at the peak, 40 held, 160 openings refused and 362 returns to a closed chat by 23:00; 4-bit weights about 4 GB, 51 GB of room, 51 chats; cold case 4,000-token chats, 250 pages, 81 fit, 39 paused at the peak for up to 9 min 45 s, two cards 163, 4 bits 104. Price $2.79 a card hour (Lambda's list, read 16 October 2026), $2,037 a 730-hour month. Timeline: the program written in 2024, the longest allowed chat 2,048 tokens until Monday 24 August 2026, raised that day to 8,192 at the procedures engineer's request; normal nights since then at most 30 open chats (30 GB); the sizing sheet signed Thursday 27 August, after the raise, from the program's count of 24 to 26 August, which showed the average chat unchanged; the shutdown began Monday 14 September for five weeks (to Sunday 18 October); 22:10 the 41st contractor refused; 22:15 contractors crowd the permit cabin holding phones that say busy (the alert); crews work from printed procedures until 06:00; the post at about 06:15 on Tuesday 15 September. Cold case: 3 months later, 14 September to Monday 14 December 2026 (the engine live from Tuesday 15 September; the shutdown ended Sunday 18 October; whole procedures attached from November; the January sheet signed Thursday 10 December). Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: What It Keeps in Mind

post.author: u/permit_cabin_hrafnhild
post.title: I sign the night permits during our refinery's shutdown. At 22:10 the assistant told the 41st contractor it was busy. Its own count said the chats filled 19.5% of their room.

blocks.text: I'm Hrafnhild, night permit coordinator at the Grisholme oil refinery. On Monday 14 September the plant began its planned five-week maintenance shutdown: units emptied, opened, inspected and repaired, with 400 contractors on nights. No job starts until I sign its permit.
Contractors ask our procedures assistant how each job is done. It's a language model, a program that writes text in small pieces called tokens. Each conversation with it is a chat.
Ours is Llama 3.1 8B, on one rented graphics card, a card for short: an NVIDIA A100 80GB, $2.79 an hour. Its weights, the model's learned numbers, take 15 GB of the card's 80 GB of memory.
While it writes, the model keeps notes on every token of the chat so far, like a crew's handover notes, so it never has to read the whole chat again. Those notes are the chat's working memory.

They grow one token at a time. Each new token passes through the model's 32 layers, its stacked stages. At every layer it leaves a key and a value, the label and contents other tokens look up (case a1e05): 8 lists each, 128 numbers a list, 2 bytes a number. By hand: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KB a token.
The card's meter counts 1,024 bytes to a KB, 1,024 KB to an MB and 1,024 MB to a GB.

The program that runs the model on the card was written in 2024 by a contractor, Ambrogio. When a chat opens, it reserves room on the card for the longest chat allowed. When the chat closes, it frees that room.
Until Monday 24 August the longest allowed chat was 2,048 tokens: 256 MB a chat. That day it went up to 8,192, so engineers could paste long procedures: 8,192 × 128 KB = 1 GB a chat.

The card also runs the document-search model, which takes 24 GB. Ours may use the other 56: 15 for weights, 1 of working space for sums in progress, 40 for chats. Since the raise, normal nights have had at most 30 chats open.

blocks.title: SIZING SHEET · night shutdown, procedures assistant
items: Chats: about 4 a minute from 22:00, each open about 30 minutes, so 120 open at the peak
Average chat: 1,600 tokens (the program's count, 24 to 26 August) × 128 KB = 200 MB
Room for chats: 40 GB ÷ 200 MB = 204 chats. Enough.

blocks.text: Ugochukwu, our shutdown planner, signed it three days after the raise. The program's count showed the average chat unchanged, so he used it.

On the first night, chats opened at 4 a minute from 22:00, as the sheet said. Each line below shows the time, the card's own memory meter, and the program's count of open chats, tokens held and room used.

22:09:45  card meter  80 of 80 GB (100%)   program  40 chats  64,000 tokens  7.8 of 40 GB (19.5%)
22:10:00  chat 41 refused: assistant busy, try later
At 22:15 the permit cabin filled with contractors holding up phones that all said busy.
By then 21 had been turned away. In the first hour 240 of our 400 asked, and 160 were refused. We worked from printed procedures until 06:00.

Middle row: the document-search model, 24 GB; the weights, 15 GB; working space, 1 GB; the chat room, 40 GB reserved, 40 chats of 1 GB. Bottom row, under the chat room: held, 64,000 tokens, 7.8 GB, 19.5% of the room; reserved but empty, 32.2 GB, 80.5%.

blocks.text: By hand: 40 chats × 1 GB reserved = 40 GB, all of it. Held: 64,000 tokens × 128 KB = 7.8 GB, 19.5%. We pay $2.79 an hour for a card whose chat room is four-fifths empty.
Ugochukwu says the meter says full, so we buy another card. The next night shift starts at 22:00. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that cabin is haunted, though a room of phones all saying busy is grim. Your chat's working memory has a name: the KV cache, short for key-value cache, a store kept close at hand of every token's keys and values (a1e09's cache was the same idea). Llama's makers kept only 8 key-value lists per layer to make it smaller. Two questions. Of the 40 GB your program had reserved at 22:10, how much held real tokens? And how much does it reserve for a chat holding 1,600 tokens, against what the sheet counted?

replies.author: u/permit_cabin_hrafnhild
replies.text: 7.8 GB held real tokens, 19.5%. A 1,600-token chat gets the same 1 GB as one at 8,192. The sheet counted 200 MB.

comments.author: u/full_means_full_ugochukwu
comments.text: I signed the sheet, from the program's own count. The card's meter says 100%. Full means full: whatever the program does inside, the card has no room left. So rent a second card, run the same program on it, and that's 40 more chats tomorrow night. Two cards at $5.58 an hour, against 160 contractors at the cabin door.

replies.author: u/permit_cabin_hrafnhild
replies.text: The same program, with the same settings?

replies.author: u/full_means_full_ugochukwu
replies.text: Copied as it is. Nothing new to test, and it's live by tonight.

comments.author: u/wrote_it_in_2024_ambrogio
comments.text: I wrote the program. Reserving the longest chat up front was deliberate: a chat can never run out of room halfway through an answer. Newer programs hand room out in pages instead, like a notebook given a page at a time. A chat starts with one page of 16 tokens and gets another each time one fills, and a table records where each page sits on the card. When the card is full, they pause the newest chat and resume it later. I'd rather tell a contractor busy than leave them stuck halfway through a procedure. It has run since 2024 without refusing anyone.

comments.author: u/long_procedures_tiwalade
comments.text: Procedures engineer. I asked for 8,192 so crews could paste a whole isolation procedure, and they do. Don't take it away. Most of those 40 chats sat idle anyway, open with nobody typing in them. Close any chat left idle for five minutes and give its room to the next contractor.

replies.author: u/permit_cabin_hrafnhild
replies.text: Contractors ask, then go and do the step, about ten minutes, then ask the next thing.

reply.prompt: It's 06:30 on Tuesday 15 September, and the next night shift starts at 22:00. What should the refinery change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Rent a second card running the same program, to hold 40 more chats at once.
options.verdict: Twice the bill, the same waste
options.part2: On Tuesday IT rented a second A100 and copied the program with its settings, so it set aside 56 GB on the new card too. At 22:00 the two cards held 80 chats between them, for $5.58 an hour. At the peak 120 contractors wanted a chat: 40 had been refused by 22:45 and 80 by 23:00, half as many as Monday. The program's count on both cards read 19.5% in use. We were paying twice for room that was four-fifths empty.
options.senior: The card's meter counts memory that is set aside as used, so full meant reserved, not filled. A second card running the same program reserves the same 1 GB per chat and copies the waste: 80 chats at 19.5% in use, for twice the bill. Look at what the chats actually hold before buying memory.

options.text: Put the longest allowed chat back to 2,048 tokens, as it was before August.
options.part2: On Tuesday the limit went back to 2,048 tokens. That night the program reserved 256 MB a chat, so 160 fit. At the peak 120 were open: 30 GB reserved, 23.4 GB used, 78.1%. Nobody was refused, and the cabin stayed quiet. But at 23:20 a crew pasted a long isolation procedure and the assistant cut it off at 2,048 tokens, so Tiwalade's engineers went back to printing procedures. And every chat still sets aside the most it could ever need, so the next raise brings the crowd back.
options.senior: An honest trade. It buys room by taking away the long chats the engineers asked for, and the sheet still overcounts (204 against 160), though 160 covers tonight's 120. The waste stays: every chat reserves the longest it could become. Good as a one-night stopgap, not as the fix.

options.text: Close any chat left idle for five minutes, to free the room it reserved.
options.part2: From Tuesday the program closed any chat idle for five minutes. Contractors ask, then spend about ten minutes on the job, so every chat closed before its next question. At the peak 60 wanted a chat at once instead of 120, but only 40 fit, because each still reserved 1 GB at 19.5% in use. By 23:00, 160 openings had been refused, and contractors had come back to a closed chat 362 times, each time pasting their procedure again.
options.senior: Closing idle chats frees room by throwing away working memory the contractor still needs, and it leaves the reservation untouched: 1 GB a chat, 19.5% in use. It swaps a memory problem for a lost-thread problem. The waste is in how much each chat sets aside, not in how long it stays open.

options.text: Hand out memory in 16-token pages as each chat grows; pause, not refuse.
options.part2: On Tuesday IT installed vLLM, a free serving engine that hands out pages, on the same card, set to the same 56 GB, with the 8,192 limit kept and pausing on. By 18:00 they had replayed Monday's first hour in the sim: 327,680 tokens of room, 20,480 pages of 16, about 204 average chats. At 22:00 chats opened at 4 a minute again. At the peak, 22:45, 120 were open, holding 192,000 tokens in 23.4 GB of pages. Nobody was refused and nobody paused. Tiwalade's crews pasted whole procedures. The card still costs $2.79 an hour; it now carries three times as many chats.
options.senior: Size working memory by what chats hold, not by what they might become. The KV cache costs 128 KB a token here, so 40 GB holds 327,680 tokens. Reserving the longest chat at open hands each chat 1 GB whether it holds 1,600 tokens or 8,192, and most of it sits empty: 19.5% in use here, 20.4% to 38.2% in the PagedAttention paper's measurements of older systems. Handing out 16-token pages as chats grow, with a table of where each page sits, fits about 204 average chats; when the card does fill, pausing the newest and resuming it later beats refusing. The price: a full card makes some chats wait, so you still size for the peak.

sim.title: Plan the chat memory for the first shutdown night
sim.lede: You're Hrafnhild at 21:55 on Monday 14 September, before the first shutdown night shift. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 8B keeps 2 × 32 layers × 8 lists × 128 numbers × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, 128 KB, of working memory per token; one A100 80GB, with 24 GB for the document-search model, 15 for the weights (about 4 in 4 bits), 1 of working space and the rest for chats (40 GB). The refinery's own figures: 240 of the 400 night contractors open a chat in the first hour, 4 a minute from 22:00, each open 30 minutes; open chats average 1,600 tokens, and the sim counts every open chat at that average; a contractor asks something about every 10 minutes. The old program reserves the whole longest allowed chat when a chat opens and refuses when the room is all reserved. Pages hand out 16 tokens at a time as a chat grows; when the card is full the newest chat is paused and resumed when room frees, oldest first. Card price $2.79 an hour.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is 22:10 as the night will run it: 40 chats of 1 GB, 64,000 tokens, 7.8 of 40 GB, 19.5%, the 41st refused, against the sheet's 204. Play the night: 21 refused by 22:15, 120 wanted at 22:45, 160 of 240 refused by 23:00. Set the longest chat to 2,048: 160 fit. Back to 8,192 and switch to pages: 327,680 tokens, about 204 average chats, all 120 held at the peak. Try two cards, idle close and 4-bit weights. Then set the average chat to 4,000 tokens with pages and watch who waits. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the cabin was haunted. The program reserved room for the longest allowed chat, 8,192 tokens × 128 KB = 1 GB, the moment each chat opened, so 40 GB held 40 chats. Those chats averaged 1,600 tokens, 64,000 in all, 7.8 GB: 19.5% of what was reserved. The sizing sheet counted chats as they are, 200 MB each, 204 in 40 GB; the program reserves them as they might become.

steps.title: The chat's working memory: 128 KB a token.
steps.text: First, the model reads the chat's tokens. Second, at each of its 32 layers it works out every token's key and value, the label and contents later tokens look up. Third, it keeps them, so each new token can look back without the whole chat being read again. Fourth, each token it writes adds its own key and value at every layer. Engineers call this store the KV cache. Llama 3.1 8B keeps 8 key-value lists per layer, 128 numbers each, 2 bytes a number: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KB a token. Its makers share each key-value list among several query lists (grouped query attention) to shrink this; the PagedAttention paper's OPT-13B, which does not, needs 800 KB a token. a1e09 was about what the model can see; this is where the card keeps it. What can go wrong: forgetting that every token of every open chat holds room on the card.

steps.title: Memory math: weights, working space, then chats.
steps.text: The card's 80 GB: 24 for the document-search model, 15 for the weights, 1 of working space, 40 for chats. 40 GB is 41,943,040 KB; at 128 KB a token that is 327,680 tokens. The sheet divided by the average chat: 1,600 × 128 KB = 200 MB, so 40,960 MB ÷ 200 = 204 chats. The program divides by what it sets aside: 8,192 × 128 KB = 1 GB, so 40. Before 24 August, at 2,048 tokens, it set aside 256 MB, so 160 fit, and since the raise normal nights stayed at 30 or fewer. What can go wrong: a sum that is right about the chats and wrong about the program.

steps.title: Reserving the longest chat: room set aside, not filled.
steps.text: First, a chat opens. Second, the program sets aside room for 8,192 tokens in one unbroken stretch, 1 GB. Third, the chat fills part of it, 1,600 tokens on average, 200 MB. Fourth, when the chat closes the 1 GB is freed. At 22:09:45, 40 chats held 64,000 tokens, 7.8 GB of 40 reserved: 19.5%. The card's meter counts set-aside memory as used, so it read 80 of 80 GB. Kwon and colleagues measured older serving systems working this way with only 20.4% to 38.2% of this memory holding real tokens. What can go wrong: a meter that says full over a room that is four-fifths empty.

steps.title: Pages: room handed out as each chat grows.
steps.text: First, a new chat gets one page: room for 16 tokens, 16 × 128 KB = 2 MB, wherever a free page sits. Second, when that page fills, it gets another. Third, a table for each chat records where its pages are, so the pages need not sit side by side, like a notebook given a page at a time. Fourth, when the chat closes its pages go back. Fifth, if no page is free, the engine as the refinery set it up pauses the newest chat, frees its pages, and later resumes it; vLLM rebuilds the paused chat's working memory from its text. 40 GB is 20,480 pages, about 204 chats of 1,600 tokens; at the peak 120 held 192,000 tokens in 23.4 GB. Only each chat's last page can be part-empty. What can go wrong: when chats grow longer, fewer fit, and the rest wait.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fall short.
steps.text: A second card with the same program sets aside 1 GB a chat on both: 80 chats, $5.58 an hour, still 19.5% in use, 80 refused by 23:00. Closing chats idle for five minutes cuts the peak to 60 wanted, but only 40 fit, and contractors came back to a closed chat 362 times. The 2,048 limit fits 160 and cuts off long procedures. Storing the weights in 4 bits (INT4, whole numbers 4 bits long) shrinks them to about 4 GB: 51 GB of room, 51 chats of 1 GB, from a model nobody has tested, which a later case in this season measures. What can go wrong: buying or freeing memory before checking how it is handed out.

diagram.aria: Two ways to hand out room for a chat. Top row, the old program: a chat opens with 1,600 tokens; the program reserves 8,192 × 128 KB, 1 GB, at once; the chat holds 1,600 tokens, 200 MB used; 40 GB holds 40 chats, 19.5% in use. Bottom row, pages: a chat opens; it gets one 16-token page, 2 MB; it gets a page each time one fills, with a table of its pages; 40 GB holds about 204 average chats, and when full the newest is paused.

notes.text: Whole chat at open: 40 x 1 GB, 7.8 GB used, 19.5%
Pages as it grows: 327,680 tokens, about 204 chats
Each token keeps 128 KB, wherever it is kept

explain.caption: Read each row left to right. The old program sets aside a whole 8,192-token chat, 1 GB, the moment a chat opens, though the average chat fills 200 MB of it, so 40 GB holds 40 chats. Pages hand out 2 MB at a time as a chat grows, with a table of where each page sits, so the same 40 GB holds about 204 average chats.

fix.title: The fix: hand out room in 16-token pages as each chat grows, and pause instead of refusing
fix.text: Serve the model with an engine that hands out working memory in 16-token pages, such as vLLM, on the same card and the same 56 GB. Keep the 8,192 limit, so engineers can still paste long procedures. Turn pausing on: when no page is free, the newest chat waits and resumes when room frees, instead of being refused. Rebuild the sizing sheet with the sum the engine uses: 40 GB ÷ 128 KB = 327,680 tokens, divided by the average open chat, measured again before each shutdown. Watch two numbers on the night, chats paused and the longest pause, and tell the permit coordinator when either rises, before the cabin fills.

limits: Pages fit chats as they are, so the number that fits moves with the average chat. Chats twice as long fit half as many, and a full card makes the newest wait. Re-measure the average before each big night.

Only each chat's last page can be part-empty, up to 15 tokens of 16, so a real engine lands just under the sim's 100%. Pausing also costs time: the paused chat's working memory is rebuilt when it resumes.
The 1,600-token average, the 4 chats a minute and the 30 minutes are the refinery's own figures. Another site, model or card needs its own: the 128 KB a token holds only for Llama 3.1 8B in 16 bits.
explain.seniorTake: Every token a model keeps in a chat costs memory on the card: its key and value at every layer, 128 KB a token for Llama 3.1 8B in 16 bits. Memory math is weights, plus working space, plus open chats times tokens times that cost, and the last term must be what the serving program actually sets aside, not what the chats hold. A program that reserves the longest possible chat when it opens sets aside 1 GB for a chat that fills 200 MB, so the card fills at 19.5% in use while its meter reads 100%. Hand out working memory in small pages as each chat grows, keep a table of where each page sits, and the same room holds about five times as many chats; when the card does fill, pause the newest and resume it later. The sheet counted chats as they are; the program reserved them as they might become. Size for the first, and choose a program that behaves that way.

realWorld.title: PagedAttention: room reserved for the maximum length
realWorld.text: Kwon and colleagues' paper on serving large language models with PagedAttention says that existing systems pre-allocate a contiguous chunk of memory with the request’s maximum length, and that only 20.4% - 38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store the actual token states in the existing systems. The refinery's old program did the same and landed at 19.5%.

realWorld.title: PagedAttention: blocks of 16, like pages
realWorld.text: The same paper hands out the KV cache in blocks as each request grows, and its block manager keeps a table for each request of where its blocks sit. It says one can think of blocks as pages, tokens as bytes, and requests as processes, and that vLLM sets its default block size as 16. For its OPT-13B model it notes that the KV cache of a single token demands 800 KB of space; Llama 3.1 8B needs 128 KB.

realWorld.title: vLLM: pause, then recompute
realWorld.text: vLLM's Optimization and Tuning page says that when KV cache space is insufficient, vLLM can preempt requests to free up KV cache space for other requests, and that Preempted requests are recomputed when sufficient KV cache space becomes available again. It adds that preemption and recomputation can adversely affect end-to-end latency. Pausing beats refusing, but it is not free.

realWorld.title: Llama 3: fewer key-value lists, a smaller cache
realWorld.text: The Llama 3 paper's table of settings gives the 8B model 32 layers, a model dimension of 4,096 and 8 key/value heads. It says the models use grouped query attention (GQA) with 8 key-value heads to improve inference speed and to reduce the size of key-value caches during decoding. That is why a token costs 128 KB here and not four times as much.

realWorld.title: What an hour of the card costs
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA A100 SXM with 80 GB (SXM is the board form the card is built in) at $2.79 per GPU per hour. At that price the refinery's card is about $2,037 a 730-hour month, and a second card running the same program doubles it for 80 chats at 19.5% in use. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

asked: How much KV cache memory does a model need per token?
interview.answer: Per token, the KV cache holds a key and a value at every layer for every key-value head: 2 × layers × key-value heads × numbers per head × bytes per number. For Llama 3.1 8B in 16 bits that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KB; models without grouped query attention cost far more, like OPT-13B's 800 KB. Then memory math: card memory minus weights minus working space is the room for the cache, and room ÷ bytes per token is how many tokens all open chats can hold, here 40 GB ÷ 128 KB = 327,680 tokens. PagedAttention solves how that room is handed out. Older servers pre-allocate one unbroken stretch for each request's maximum length, so most of it sits empty: the paper measured 20.4% to 38.2% in use, and I once saw a home-made server refuse the 41st chat at 19.5%, with 1 GB set aside for chats averaging 200 MB. PagedAttention gives each request fixed blocks, 16 tokens in vLLM, as it grows, with a block table mapping them, so the same memory holds about five times as many average chats. When memory does run out, the engine preempts a running request (in that refinery's set-up, the newest) and recomputes it later, which costs latency but refuses nobody.

terms.def: A plant that turns crude oil into fuels and other products through units of pipes, vessels and columns. Grisholme is one.
A planned stop of a whole plant so units can be emptied, opened, inspected and repaired. Grisholme's runs five weeks from Monday 14 September 2026, with 400 contractors on nights.
The paper that says a job is safe to begin, signed before any work starts. During the shutdown Hrafnhild signs the night's permits.
The person who checks and signs every job's permit through the night shift, from the permit cabin. Hrafnhild is Grisholme's.
A worker from an outside firm hired for the shutdown. 400 work nights; 240 asked the assistant in the first hour of the first night.
The written steps for a job, such as how to isolate and open a vessel. Engineers paste long ones into chats, which is why the longest chat was raised.
The steps that cut a piece of plant off from everything that could flow into it before anyone opens it.
The refinery's language model that answers contractors' questions about how each job is done, one chat per conversation.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). An average open chat here holds 1,600.
One conversation between a contractor and the assistant, kept open while the contractor works. Its tokens grow with every question and answer.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Llama 3.1 8B's take 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter.
Meta's open-weights language model with 8.03 billion weights, 32 layers and 8 key-value lists per layer (a10e01).
Short for graphics card: a board with a GPU, a graphics processing unit, and its own memory (a10e01). The refinery rents one A100 80GB at $2.79 an hour.
A graphics card with 80 GB of memory. Grisholme's is shared: 24 GB for the document-search model, 56 GB for the assistant's program.
A byte is 8 bits. On the card's meter 1 KB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MB = 1,024 KB and 1 GB = 1,024 MB. One token's working memory is 131,072 bytes, 128 KB.
The card's own report of how much memory is set aside, by any program, used or not. At 22:09:45 it read 80 of 80 GB.
Here, the serving program: the software that loads the model on the card, takes chats and hands out room for them. Ambrogio wrote the old one in 2024.
One of the model's stacked stages; every token passes through all of them in turn. Llama 3.1 8B has 32.
Two lists of numbers a token leaves at each layer: the label other tokens match against and the contents they take (a1e05).
Each layer's sets of keys and values, also called key/value heads. Llama 3.1 8B keeps 8 per layer, 128 numbers each.
Here, the keys and values the model keeps for every token of a chat, so it never has to read the whole chat again. 128 KB a token for Llama 3.1 8B.
Short for key-value cache: the engineers' name for a chat's working memory on the card. It grows by 128 KB with every token here.
A store of results kept close at hand so work can be skipped (a1e09), like keeping a pot of coffee warm.
The most tokens one chat may hold. 2,048 until Monday 24 August 2026, then 8,192 so engineers could paste long procedures.
To set room aside for a chat before it needs it. The old program reserves the longest allowed chat when a chat opens: 1 GB at 8,192 tokens.
Room the program keeps for sums in progress while the model runs, separate from chats: 1 GB here.
A second model on the same card that finds documents for staff. It takes 24 GB, which is why the assistant's program may use only 56.
Ugochukwu's plan of how many chats the card holds, signed Thursday 27 August: 40 GB ÷ 200 MB average chat = 204.
The mean number of tokens in an open chat, from the program's own count: 1,600 tokens, 200 MB of working memory.
The most chats wanted at once. The sheet's: 4 chats a minute × 30 minutes open = 120, reached from 22:30.
A chat that is open with nobody typing in it, usually because the contractor is doing the step it explained.
Card memory = weights + working space + open chats × tokens × memory per token. Here 15 + 1 + 40 GB, and 40 GB ÷ 128 KB = 327,680 tokens.
A small fixed block of working memory, room for 16 tokens, 2 MB here, handed to a chat when it needs more. Like a notebook given a page at a time.
The record, one per chat, of where each of its pages sits on the card, so the pages need not sit side by side. The paper calls it a block table.
When no page is free, the engine stops the newest chat, frees its pages, and resumes it when room returns. Engineers call it preemption.
How vLLM resumes a paused chat: it works out the chat's keys and values again from its text, which takes a little time.
Handing out a model's working memory in small pages as each chat grows, with a table of where they sit. vLLM's version is PagedAttention.
A free, widely used serving engine for language models, built around PagedAttention, with 16-token pages by default.
Letting several query lists share one key-value list, so fewer keys and values are kept. Llama 3.1 8B keeps 8 per layer, not 32.
An older open model the PagedAttention paper uses as an example: 800 KB of working memory a token, against Llama 3.1 8B's 128 KB.
Short for 4-bit integer: storing each weight as a whole number 4 bits long. Llama 3.1 8B's weights would take about 4 GB, but the model would need testing.
The engineers' word for pausing a running request to free memory for others; vLLM recomputes it later.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A control 8.6 covers capacity management.
Making sure systems have the resources the work needs, now and later, by monitoring, testing and planning.
A US auditing report on a service's controls, judged against the trust services criteria of the AICPA, the US accountants' body; A1.1 covers processing capacity.

atWork: Look for a home-made or older serving program that sets aside room for the longest allowed request when it starts, and a sizing sheet built from the average request. It is a common pattern: the program refuses users with most of its memory empty, and the card's meter says full. Ask four things. How many bytes of working memory does one token cost for your model, layers × key-value lists × numbers × bytes × 2? What does the program set aside per request, the longest allowed or what the request holds? What share of what it sets aside holds real tokens at your busiest hour? And when memory runs out, does it refuse, or pause and resume? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.6 (capacity management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for a sizing sheet that matches how the program actually reserves memory, re-checked after changes such as a longer limit; and if you report against SOC 2, an auditor checking criterion A1.1 (processing capacity, as quoted by a third-party guide) would look for the same, plus monitoring of refused or paused requests. Neither note is legal advice.

recall.prompt: A bank's helpdesk serves Llama 3.1 8B on a home-made program with 20 GB for conversations. Requests may grow to 4,096 tokens; the program's count says open ones average 1,024. It turns users away at 40 open, and the card's meter reads full. The team wants a second card. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Each request is given room for its maximum up front: 4,096 × 128 KB = 512 MB, so 20 GB holds 40
Only a quarter of that holds real tokens: 1,024 × 128 KB = 128 MB each, 5 GB of 20, 25%
Hand out memory in small pages as each request grows (paged attention, vLLM): 163,840 tokens, about 160 average requests, and pause instead of turning away

recall.model: Don't buy a card yet. The program sets aside room for the maximum when each request opens: 4,096 tokens × 128 KB = 512 MB, so 20 GB holds 40, and the meter counts that as full. But open requests average 1,024 tokens, 128 MB each, so the 40 hold 5 GB of the 20: a quarter, 25%, the rest unused. Serve with an engine that hands out memory in small pages as each request grows, like vLLM's paged attention: 20 GB ÷ 128 KB = 163,840 tokens, about 160 average requests, and when it is full it pauses the newest instead of turning users away. A second card running the same program would only double the waste.

recall.prompt: Llama 3.1 8B keeps 128 KB of working memory per token. The longest allowed chat is 8,192 tokens. How much does a program that reserves the longest chat set aside when a chat opens?
recall.why: 8,192 × 128 KB = 1,048,576 KB = 1 GB, whatever the chat later holds. 200 MB is the average 1,600-token chat, what the sizing sheet counted; 256 MB is the old 2,048-token limit.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what problem does PagedAttention solve, and how?

keyIdeas.idea: Older servers give each request one unbroken stretch of memory sized for its maximum length, so most of the KV cache sits empty (20.4% to 38.2% in use in the paper)
It hands out memory in fixed blocks (16 tokens in vLLM) as each request grows, with a block table mapping where each block sits
So far more requests fit in the same memory, and when it runs out the newest is preempted and recomputed rather than refused

recall.model: Each request's KV cache, the keys and values kept for every token, grows as the answer is written, and older servers pre-allocated one unbroken stretch for each request's maximum length. Most of it sat empty: the PagedAttention paper measured only 20.4% to 38.2% in use. PagedAttention hands out the cache in fixed blocks, 16 tokens in vLLM, as each request grows, wherever a free block is, with a block table recording where each one sits, like pages of a notebook. So far more requests fit in the same memory, and when it does run out, the engine can preempt the newest request and recompute it later instead of refusing it.

recall.prompt: 40 GB is set aside for chats, each token keeps 128 KB, and memory is handed out in 16-token pages. About how many 1,600-token chats fit?
recall.why: 40 GB ÷ 128 KB = 327,680 tokens, or 20,480 pages of 16. A 1,600-token chat is 100 pages, so 204 fit. 40 is what reserving 8,192 tokens a chat gives; 160 is reserving 2,048.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Since Tuesday 15 September the assistant has run on vLLM with 16-token pages and the 8,192 limit. The shutdown ended on Sunday 18 October without one refusal. In November the procedures team began attaching each job's whole isolation procedure to its chat, and the program's count now puts the average open chat at 4,000 tokens. On Thursday 10 December Ugochukwu signed the sheet for a two-week unit shutdown in January: 4 chats a minute again, each open 30 minutes, 120 at the peak. His note: the engine holds 204 chats, nothing to change.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Does the card hold 204 chats in January? What happens at the peak, and what would you change before then?

keyIdeas.idea: Not 204: 4,000 × 128 KB = 500 MB a chat (250 pages), so 327,680 tokens hold about 81
At the peak 120 want a chat, 81 are held and 39 are paused, nobody refused, the longest wait about ten minutes
Re-size from the new average and add room before January: a second card holds about 163, or trim what is attached to each chat

coldCase.model: No. The 204 was 327,680 tokens ÷ 1,600. At the new average, 4,000 × 128 KB = 500 MB a chat, 250 pages, so the card holds about 81. At the peak 120 want a chat: 81 are held and 39 are paused. Nobody is refused, but in the sim the 39 wait their turn, up to 9 min 45 s, until the first chats close at 22:30. Before January, re-size from the new average and add room: a second card on the same engine holds 655,360 tokens, about 163 chats, enough for 120; or trim what is attached so chats stay shorter. Storing the weights in 4 bits would give 104, from a model nobody has tested.
